Definition: from G3713; properly, desire (as a reaching forth or excitement of the mind), i.e. (by analogy), violent passion (ire, or (justifiable) abhorrence); by implication punishment:--anger, indignation, vengeance, wrath.
BiblicalUsage: Wrath in the New Testament is both human and divine, and the difference matters. Paul tells believers to lift up holy hands without wrath, and warns that the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience, while remembering that we were by nature children of wrath, and Jesus delivers us from the wrath to come.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that the wrath of God is real, and that is exactly why the gospel is good news: Jesus delivers us from the wrath to come, and I do not need to earn my way out of it. That is why I do not fear God's wrath the way I fear man's: His is just, and Jesus has already borne it for me.
